q: Which of the following is a core principle of green chemistry?
o: Maximise use of hazardous solvents for speed
Use stoichiometric reagents instead of catalysts
Prevent waste rather than treat it after formation
why: Green chemistry's first principle is to design processes that prevent waste from forming at all.

q: Using hydrogen peroxide instead of chlorine-based bleach is considered a green chemistry choice because
o: H2O2 gives only water as the by-product
H2O2 is a stronger oxidant than chlorine
Chlorine bleach has higher atom economy
why: Hydrogen peroxide oxidation produces only water as by-product, reducing hazardous waste compared to chlorine-based bleaching.

q: In the green synthesis of adipic acid, using H2O2 with a catalyst instead of nitric acid oxidation mainly avoids the release of
why: Traditional nitric acid oxidation of cyclohexanone releases polluting N2O gas, which the H2O2-based green route avoids.

q: Atom economy of a reaction is calculated as
o: (mass of waste / mass of product) x 100
(mass of desired product / total mass of reactants) x 100
(mass of reactants / mass of product) x 100
why: Atom economy percentage compares the molar mass of the desired product to the total molar mass of all reactants.

q: For a reaction A + B -> C (desired) + D, if molar mass of C is 90 and total reactant mass is 120, the atom economy is
Addition reactions generally have an atom economy of approximately
why: In addition reactions no atoms are lost as by-products, so essentially all reactant atoms end up in the product (100%).

q: Compared to bulk gold, gold nanoparticles typically appear
o: Red/purple due to size-dependent optical properties
why: At the nanoscale, quantum size effects change light absorption, so gold nanoparticles appear red/purple instead of golden yellow.
